topic: String, immutability, and the string pool

questions.title: String Literal vs Constructor Allocation
questions.question: Create a string using a string literal and another using the `new String()` constructor, and print both to illustrate instantiation syntax.
questions.explanation: In Java, strings can be instantiated either as string literals or as explicit heap objects via the `new` keyword[cite: 18]. When a string literal like `"Java Programming"` is encountered, the JVM checks the String Constant Pool (SCP) in the Java heap[cite: 18]. If the literal is already present, the existing reference is reused[cite: 18]. In contrast, using `new String("Java Programming")` forces the JVM to allocate a distinct new `String` object in general heap memory, even if an identical character sequence already resides in the pool[cite: 18]. Both instances reference internal byte arrays containing the characters, but their reference addresses differ[cite: 18]. Understanding this distinction is foundational for memory optimization and avoiding unintentional object duplication in enterprise applications[cite: 18].
hints: Declare one string using quotes: `String s1 = "Java Programming";`[cite: 18].
Declare the second string explicitly: `String s2 = new String("Java Programming");`[cite: 18].
Print both variables to confirm identical content representation[cite: 18].
questions.expectedOutput:
Literal String: Java Programming
Object String:  Java Programming

questions.title: String Traversal and Length Inspection
questions.question: Print the length of a string and display each character on a new line using a loop and `charAt()`.
questions.explanation: A Java `String` is an indexed, zero-based sequence of characters[cite: 18]. The `.length()` method returns the total number of UTF-16 code units in the string[cite: 8]. To access individual characters at specific offsets, the `.charAt(int index)` method retrieves the character at the specified position[cite: 18]. Passing an index outside the range `[0, length() - 1]` causes the JVM to throw a `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`. Inside a `for` loop running from index 0 to `length() - 1`, `charAt(i)` visits each character in sequential order[cite: 14, 18]. This mechanical traversal forms the basis for string parsing, validation, and character frequency analysis algorithms.
hints: Query the string size using `str.length()`[cite: 8, 18].
Iterate with `for (int i = 0; i < str.length(); i++)`[cite: 14, 18].
Extract each character using `str.charAt(i)` and print it[cite: 18].
questions.expectedOutput:
String: Java
Length: 4
J
a
v
a

questions.title: String Concatenation: Operator vs Method
questions.question: Demonstrate string concatenation using both the `+` operator and the `.concat()` method, and print the results.
questions.explanation: Java offers multiple ways to concatenate character sequences[cite: 18]. The binary `+` operator is overloaded for strings; in modern Java versions (Java 9+), bytecode emission uses `invokedynamic` with `StringConcatFactory` to optimize buffer allocations dynamically[cite: 1]. The `+` operator also automatically converts non-string primitives and objects to strings, and handles `null` references by converting them to the literal text `"null"`[cite: 1, 18]. In contrast, the `str.concat(other)` method performs explicit string chaining by allocating a new byte array containing the combined character contents[cite: 18]. Unlike `+`, calling `.concat(null)` throws a `NullPointerException` because the method expects a non-null parameter[cite: 7, 18].
hints: Concatenate using the operator: `String r1 = "Hello " + "Java";`[cite: 18].
Concatenate using the method: `String r2 = "Hello ".concat("Java");`[cite: 18].
Print both variables to verify identical output[cite: 18].
questions.expectedOutput:
Using +: Hello Java
Using concat(): Hello Java

questions.title: String Literal Reference and Value Equality
questions.question: Compare two identical string literals using both `==` and `.equals()` and print both evaluation results.
questions.explanation: Understanding the difference between `==` and `.equals()` is essential in Java[cite: 5, 18]. The relational operator `==` tests reference identity—whether two references point to the exact same memory address on the heap[cite: 5, 18]. In contrast, `.equals()` evaluates content equivalence by comparing the characters sequentially[cite: 5, 18]. When two identical string literals (e.g., `s1 = "Java"` and `s2 = "Java"`) are defined, the compiler stores a single copy in the String Constant Pool[cite: 18]. Both variables receive the exact same reference address from the pool, so both `s1 == s2` and `s1.equals(s2)` evaluate to `true`[cite: 18].
hints: Declare two variables pointing to identical literals: `String s1 = "Java"; String s2 = "Java";`[cite: 18].
Evaluate reference equality using `s1 == s2`[cite: 18].
Evaluate value equality using `s1.equals(s2)`[cite: 18].
questions.expectedOutput:
s1 == s2: true
s1.equals(s2): true

questions.title: Heap String vs Literal Equality Comparison
questions.question: Compare a string created via `new String("Java")` with a string literal `"Java"` using both `==` and `.equals()`, and explain the output.
questions.explanation: This comparison illustrates the distinction between heap allocation and the String Constant Pool[cite: 18]. The literal `"Java"` resolves to a pooled reference managed by the JVM[cite: 18]. Using `new String("Java")` explicitly allocates a separate object on the normal Java heap[cite: 18]. Consequently, the reference variable for the `new` object holds a distinct memory address from the pooled literal reference[cite: 18]. Comparing them with `==` evaluates to `false` because they point to different memory addresses[cite: 18]. However, comparing them with `.equals()` evaluates to `true` because `.equals()` compares character values rather than memory addresses[cite: 18].
hints: Create a pooled literal `String literal = "Java";`[cite: 18].
Create a heap instance `String obj = new String("Java");`[cite: 18].
Print `literal == obj` and `literal.equals(obj)`[cite: 18].
questions.expectedOutput:
literal == heapObject: false
literal.equals(heapObject): true

questions.title: String Pool Reference Equality Check
questions.question: Demonstrate the difference between string literals and `new String()` objects using both `==` and `.equals()` across multiple references.
questions.explanation: String interning and reference equality demonstrate how the JVM manages string memory[cite: 18]. When three strings are created—two identical literals and one via `new String()`—two distinct memory representations exist[cite: 18]. The two literals share a single reference in the String Constant Pool, making `s1 == s2` evaluate to `true`[cite: 18]. The object created with `new String()` resides outside the pool in heap memory, so `s1 == s3` evaluates to `false`[cite: 18]. However, `.equals()` returns `true` across all pairs because the character sequences are identical[cite: 18]. Developers should always use `.equals()` for string comparisons to prevent bugs caused by reference mismatch[cite: 18].
hints: Declare two identical literals `s1` and `s2`, and an explicit heap instance `s3`[cite: 18].
Compare `s1 == s2` to demonstrate pool reuse[cite: 18].
Compare `s1 == s3` and `s1.equals(s3)` to demonstrate value equality versus reference divergence[cite: 18].
questions.expectedOutput:
s1 == s2 (both pooled): true
s1 == s3 (pool vs heap): false
s1.equals(s3) (value check): true

questions.title: Manual Interning Experiment
questions.question: Create a heap string via `new String("java")`. Call `.intern()` on it and prove identity equality with an existing literal.
questions.explanation: The `String.intern()` method provides programmatic access to the String Constant Pool[cite: 18]. When `s.intern()` is called on a heap-allocated `String` object, the JVM searches the constant pool for an equivalent character sequence[cite: 18]. If found, it returns the reference from the pool[cite: 18]. If not found, the string is added to the pool and that reference is returned[cite: 18]. Assigning `interned = heapString.intern()` retrieves the pooled canonical reference, allowing `interned == literal` to evaluate to `true`[cite: 18]. While interning can save memory in large systems by canonicalizing duplicate strings, overusing it can increase memory pressure on the JVM string table[cite: 18].
hints: Define a literal `String literal = "java";`[cite: 18].
Create an explicit heap string `String heap = new String("java");`[cite: 18].
Call `String interned = heap.intern();` and verify that `interned == literal` evaluates to `true`[cite: 18].
questions.expectedOutput:
heap == literal:     false
interned == literal: true

questions.title: Immutability Demonstration
questions.question: Demonstrate String immutability by calling `.concat()`, `.toUpperCase()`, and `.replace()` without assigning the return value, and verify that the original string remains unchanged.
questions.explanation: Strings in Java are immutable: once instantiated on the heap, their character contents cannot be altered[cite: 3, 18]. Under the hood, `String` is declared `final`, and its backing byte array (`byte[] value`) is marked `private final`[cite: 5, 10]. Any method that appears to modify a string (such as `.concat()`, `.toUpperCase()`, or `.replace()`) does not change the original string in place; instead, it allocates and returns a completely new `String` object containing the modified characters[cite: 18]. If the caller does not store the returned reference, the new object is discarded, and the original string remains unchanged[cite: 18]. This immutability ensures thread safety and allows strings to be safely shared in hash-based collections and classloaders[cite: 18].
hints: Declare `String text = "java backend";`[cite: 18].
Invoke `text.toUpperCase();` and `text.concat(" developer");` without assigning the return values[cite: 18].
Print `text` to verify that its value remains `"java backend"`[cite: 18].
questions.expectedOutput:
Original string after unassigned calls: java backend
New assigned reference: JAVA BACKEND

questions.title: String Palindrome Checker
questions.question: Check if a string is a palindrome (case-insensitive and ignoring non-alphanumeric characters) using a two-pointer comparison technique.
questions.explanation: A string is a palindrome if it reads identically forward and backward (e.g., 'madam' or 'Racecar')[cite: 12, 14, 18]. The two-pointer approach checks this symmetrically: one pointer starts at index 0 and advances right, while a second pointer starts at `length() - 1` and moves left[cite: 9, 14]. On each iteration, characters are converted to lowercase using `Character.toLowerCase()` to ensure case-insensitive comparison[cite: 8, 12]. If a character mismatch is detected at any point, the method terminates early and returns `false`[cite: 9, 14]. If the pointers meet in the middle without mismatch, the string is confirmed as a palindrome[cite: 9, 14]. This algorithm operates in $O(N)$ time and $O(1)$ auxiliary space without requiring string reversal or extra memory allocation[cite: 9, 14].
hints: Initialize two pointer indices: `int left = 0; int right = str.length() - 1;`[cite: 9, 14].
Compare characters using `Character.toLowerCase(str.charAt(left))` and `Character.toLowerCase(str.charAt(right))`[cite: 8, 12, 18].
Advance `left++` and decrement `right--` until pointers cross, returning `false` on any mismatch[cite: 9, 14].
questions.expectedOutput:
Input: madam
Is palindrome: true

questions.title: Character Category Counter
questions.question: Iterate through a string and count the number of vowels, consonants, digits, and special characters, printing each count.
questions.explanation: Classifying characters in a string is a common text processing task. Using a loop with `charAt(i)`, each character code point is evaluated against categorization rules[cite: 14, 18]. The `Character.isDigit(ch)` method identifies numeric digits ('0'–'9')[cite: 4, 17]. For alphabetic characters (`Character.isLetter(ch)`), converting to lowercase allows checking against vowel characters (`"aeiou".indexOf(lower) != -1`)[cite: 8, 12]. Any non-vowel letter is counted as a consonant[cite: 7]. Characters that are neither letters nor digits (such as spaces and punctuation) are classified as special characters[cite: 4].
hints: Use `Character.isDigit(ch)` to identify numeric characters[cite: 4, 17].
Use `Character.isLetter(ch)` to separate letters from symbols[cite: 4, 16].
Check vowels using `"aeiou".indexOf(Character.toLowerCase(ch)) != -1` and count remaining letters as consonants[cite: 8, 12].
questions.expectedOutput:
Input: Java 2026!
Vowels: 2
Consonants: 2
Digits: 4
Specials: 2

questions.title: String Interning and Identity Matching
questions.question: Demonstrate the behavior of `.intern()` by comparing `new String("java").intern()` against a string literal `"java"` using the reference equality operator (`==`).
questions.explanation: The JVM maintains a native hash map known as the String Constant Pool (SCP) to optimize memory usage by canonicalizing string literals[cite: 18]. Creating a string with `new String("java")` bypasses the pool and allocates an object in general heap memory[cite: 18]. When `.intern()` is called on that heap instance, the JVM searches the constant pool for an identical character sequence[cite: 18]. Because `"java"` already exists in the pool from literal loading, `.intern()` returns the pooled reference[cite: 18]. Consequently, `heapObj.intern() == literal` evaluates to `true`, demonstrating that `.intern()` resolves explicit heap objects back to their shared pool reference[cite: 18].
hints: Instantiate an explicit heap object: `String heapObj = new String("java");`[cite: 18].
Define an equivalent literal: `String literal = "java";`[cite: 18].
Compare `heapObj.intern() == literal` and verify it evaluates to `true`[cite: 18].
questions.expectedOutput:
heapString == literal:            false
heapString.intern() == literal:   true

questions.title: String Immutability and Reassignment Mechanics
questions.question: Demonstrate String immutability by calling `.concat()` and `.toUpperCase()` without assignment, printing the original, and then reassigning the reference to show how modified strings are captured.
questions.explanation: Because `String` objects are immutable in Java, their internal character state cannot be modified after construction[cite: 3, 18]. Calling `text.concat(" backend")` creates a new `String` object on the heap containing the combined characters[cite: 18]. If this return value is not captured, the newly created object becomes eligible for garbage collection, and the original variable continues pointing to the unmodified string[cite: 2, 18]. To reflect the transformation, the reference variable must be reassigned (`text = text.concat(...)`), pointing it to the newly created string object on the heap[cite: 18]. This pattern illustrates how reference reassignment works with immutable objects[cite: 5, 18].
hints: Call `text.concat(" backend")` without assignment and print `text`[cite: 18].
Reassign the variable: `text = text.concat(" backend");`[cite: 18].
Print `text` again to show the updated reference target[cite: 18].
questions.expectedOutput:
Without assignment: java
With assignment:    JAVA BACKEND

questions.title: Lexicographical String Array Sorting
questions.question: Sort an array of names lexicographically using `compareTo()` inside a manual bubble sort loop, and contrast with `compareToIgnoreCase()`.
questions.explanation: The `String` class implements `Comparable<String>`, providing the `.compareTo(String anotherString)` method for lexicographical comparison[cite: 12]. It compares character code points sequentially at each index[cite: 18]. If characters differ, it returns the difference between their numeric values (`this.charAt(k) - anotherString.charAt(k)`)[cite: 4, 18]. Because uppercase ASCII letters ('A'–'Z': 65–90) precede lowercase letters ('a'–'z': 97–122), `compareTo()` places all uppercase strings before lowercase ones[cite: 4, 5]. In contrast, `compareToIgnoreCase()` normalizes character cases before comparing, producing standard dictionary ordering regardless of capitalization[cite: 18].
hints: Implement a manual nested bubble sort loop over `names.length - 1` passes[cite: 3].
Compare adjacent elements using `names[j].compareTo(names[j + 1]) > 0`[cite: 3].
Swap elements using an intermediate temporary string variable[cite: 3, 5].
questions.expectedOutput:
Before: [Charlie, alice, Bob, david]
After:  [alice, Bob, Charlie, david]

questions.title: Concatenation Performance Benchmark: String vs StringBuilder
questions.question: Benchmark the performance difference between repeated string concatenation (`+=`) and `StringBuilder.append()` across 50,000 iterations using `System.nanoTime()`.
questions.explanation: Repeated string concatenation inside loops creates significant performance overhead due to immutability[cite: 3, 18]. In a loop of $N$ iterations, writing `str += "a"` causes the JVM to allocate a new `StringBuilder`, append the existing string, append the character, and allocate a new `String` object via `toString()` on every iteration[cite: 1, 3]. This copies $1 + 2 + 3 + \dots + N$ characters, resulting in $O(N^2)$ quadratic time complexity and creating thousands of short-lived heap objects[cite: 3]. In contrast, `StringBuilder` uses a mutable backing byte array that grows dynamically by geometric doubling, achieving amortized $O(1)$ append operations and $O(N)$ overall linear performance[cite: 3, 15].
hints: Time the `+=` loop using `System.nanoTime()` before and after[cite: 2].
Time the `StringBuilder` loop across the same iteration count[cite: 2].
Convert the elapsed nanosecond differences into milliseconds for readability[cite: 2].
questions.expectedOutput:
String += loop completed in:    > 0 ms
StringBuilder loop completed in: 1 ms
Efficiency verified: StringBuilder is orders of magnitude faster.

questions.title: String Palindrome Predicate Implementation
questions.question: Implement a method `isPalindrome(String s)` that verifies whether a string reads identically forward and backward, returning a boolean result.
questions.explanation: Palindrome checking tests symmetry across character sequences[cite: 14, 18]. The algorithm uses two pointers: one starting at the beginning (`left = 0`) and the other at the end (`right = s.length() - 1`)[cite: 9, 14]. While `left < right`, the characters at both pointers are compared[cite: 9, 14]. If `charAt(left) != charAt(right)`, the method returns `false` immediately[cite: 9, 14, 18]. If they match, `left` increments and `right` decrements[cite: 9, 14]. If the pointers meet without any mismatches, the string is confirmed as a palindrome and the method returns `true`[cite: 9, 14]. This approach operates in $O(N)$ time and $O(1)$ space without creating extra objects[cite: 9, 14].
hints: Initialize two indices: `int i = 0; int j = s.length() - 1;`[cite: 9, 14].
Compare characters at each step: `if (s.charAt(i) != s.charAt(j)) return false;`[cite: 9, 14, 18].
Advance pointers with `i++` and `j--` inside a `while (i < j)` loop[cite: 9, 14].
questions.expectedOutput:
Input: madam
Is palindrome: true

questions.title: String Compression (Run-Length Encoding)
questions.question: Implement basic run-length string compression (e.g., `'aabcccccaaa'` becomes `'a2b1c5a3'`). If the compressed string is not shorter than the original, return the original string.
questions.explanation: Run-length encoding (RLE) is a lossless data compression technique that replaces consecutive repeated characters with the character followed by its count[cite: 18]. The algorithm tracks an active character and a consecutive count[cite: 18]. A `StringBuilder` accumulates the compressed tokens as characters change[cite: 3, 18]. When the character at the current index differs from the previous one, the previous character and its count are appended, and the counter resets to 1[cite: 3]. After traversing the entire string, the final character and count are appended[cite: 3]. If the compressed string length is greater than or equal to the original length, the method returns the original string instead[cite: 18].
hints: Use a `StringBuilder` to build the compressed character sequence[cite: 3, 18].
Track repeating runs using a counter incremented while `str.charAt(i) == str.charAt(i - 1)`[cite: 14, 18].
Compare lengths at the end: `return compressed.length() < s.length() ? compressed.toString() : s;`[cite: 3, 18].
questions.expectedOutput:
Original:   aabcccccaaa
Compressed: a2b1c5a3

questions.title: Word Frequency Counter
questions.question: Given a sentence string, extract all words, strip punctuation, convert to lowercase, and count the frequency of each word.
questions.explanation: Text tokenization and frequency analysis combine regular expressions with map data structures[cite: 8]. First, the input string is converted to lowercase via `.toLowerCase()` to ensure case-insensitive matching[cite: 8, 12]. Next, `.replaceAll("[^a-zA-Z0-9 ]", "")` strips punctuation marks, leaving alphanumeric words separated by spaces[cite: 4, 8]. Splitting the cleaned string on whitespace (`split("\\s+")`) yields an array of word tokens[cite: 4, 8]. The tokens are counted using a `LinkedHashMap<String, Integer>`, which preserves the order in which words first appear[cite: 3].
hints: Normalize the string: `s.toLowerCase().replaceAll("[^a-z0-9\\s]", "")`[cite: 4, 8].
Tokenize using regex whitespace splitting: `clean.split("\\s+")`[cite: 4, 8].
Accumulate counts in a `Map<String, Integer>` using `map.put(w, map.getOrDefault(w, 0) + 1)`[cite: 8].
questions.expectedOutput:
Sentence: Java backend developer loves Java programming
Word counts: {java=2, backend=1, developer=1, loves=1, programming=1}

questions.title: Consecutive Duplicate Character Deduplicator
questions.question: Write a function that removes all consecutive duplicate characters from a string (e.g., `'aabbccba'` becomes `'abcba'`).
questions.explanation: Filtering consecutive duplicate characters differs from removing all duplicate occurrences across an entire string[cite: 17]. In consecutive deduplication, an element is retained as long as it differs from the immediately preceding character[cite: 18]. The algorithm initializes a `StringBuilder` with the first character of the input string[cite: 3]. A loop then inspects each subsequent character from index 1 to `length() - 1`[cite: 14, 18]. If `str.charAt(i)` differs from `str.charAt(i - 1)`, the character is appended[cite: 3, 18]. This removes adjacent repeating runs while preserving non-consecutive duplicates later in the string, operating in linear $O(N)$ time[cite: 18].
hints: Initialize a `StringBuilder` and append the first character: `sb.append(s.charAt(0))`[cite: 3, 18].
Iterate from `1` to `s.length() - 1`[cite: 14, 18].
Append `s.charAt(i)` only when it does not equal `s.charAt(i - 1)`[cite: 3, 18].
questions.expectedOutput:
Original: aabbccba
Result:   abcba

questions.title: Semantic Version Number Comparator
questions.question: Compare two version number strings (e.g., `'1.2'` vs `'1.10'`, `'1.01'` vs `'1.001'`) and determine which version is newer.
questions.explanation: Comparing software version strings requires numerical segment comparison rather than simple lexicographical sorting[cite: 18]. Lexicographically, `"1.2".compareTo("1.10")` produces an incorrect result because `'2' > '1'`[cite: 18]. A proper semantic version comparator splits version strings on dot delimiters (`split("\\.")`) and compares corresponding segments numerically using `Integer.parseInt()`[cite: 3, 8]. Segments with leading zeros (e.g., '01' and '001') parse to the same numeric value (1)[cite: 3]. If one version string has fewer segments than the other, missing segments are treated as 0[cite: 6, 9].
hints: Split version strings using regex dot delimiter: `v.split("\\.")`[cite: 7, 8].
Iterate up to `Math.max(v1Parts.length, v2Parts.length)`[cite: 3, 14].
Parse each segment with `Integer.parseInt()`, defaulting missing segments to 0[cite: 3, 6, 9].
questions.expectedOutput:
Comparing '1.2' vs '1.10': vB is newer
Comparing '1.01' vs '1.001': Versions are equal

questions.title: Compile-Time Constant Folding vs Runtime Concatenation
questions.question: Demonstrate compile-time constant folding: compare `'a' + 'b' == 'ab'` with runtime string concatenation and `final` variable concatenation to observe String Pool behavior.
questions.explanation: The Java compiler optimizes string concatenation differently depending on whether operands are compile-time constants (JLS §15.28)[cite: 6, 18]. When two string literals are concatenated (`"a" + "b"`), the compiler evaluates the expression at compile time through constant folding, emitting the pooled literal `"ab"` directly into the bytecode constant pool[cite: 1, 6, 18]. Consequently, `("a" + "b") == "ab"` evaluates to `true`[cite: 18]. The same optimization applies when concatenating `final` variables initialized with constant expressions[cite: 6, 18]. However, concatenating non-final variables involves runtime evaluation, producing a new `String` object on the heap whose reference differs from the pooled literal, making `==` evaluate to `false`[cite: 18].
hints: Test constant folding: `("a" + "b") == "ab"` evaluates to `true`[cite: 18].
Test runtime concatenation: `String a = "a"; String b = "b"; (a + b) == "ab"` evaluates to `false`[cite: 18].
Test compile-time final variables: `final String fa = "a"; final String fb = "b"; (fa + fb) == "ab"` evaluates to `true`[cite: 6, 18].
questions.expectedOutput:
("a" + "b") == "ab": true
(rA + rB) == "ab":         false
(fA + fB) == "ab":         true

questions.title: Reverse Words in a Sentence
questions.question: Reverse the order of words in a sentence string while preserving individual word character ordering and handling variable whitespace.
questions.explanation: Reversing word order in a sentence requires splitting the sentence into words while preserving the internal character sequence of each word[cite: 18]. Trimming leading and trailing whitespace with `.trim()` and splitting on the regex pattern `"\\s+"` handles multiple contiguous spaces cleanly[cite: 4, 8]. The resulting token array is traversed in reverse order—from `tokens.length - 1` down to 0—appending each word to a `StringBuilder` separated by single spaces[cite: 3, 14]. This reverses word placement while keeping individual words intact[cite: 18].
hints: Trim input and split on multiple spaces: `sentence.trim().split("\\s+")`[cite: 4, 8].
Traverse the resulting array in reverse: `for (int i = words.length - 1; i >= 0; i--)`[cite: 3, 14].
Join words using `StringBuilder` or `String.join()`[cite: 3].
questions.expectedOutput:
Original: Java Programming Language
Reversed: Language Programming Java

questions.title: Anagram Verification via Frequency Table
questions.question: Check whether two strings are anagrams of each other in $O(N)$ time using a character frequency array without sorting.
questions.explanation: Two strings are anagrams if they contain the exact same characters with identical frequencies, arranged in a different order (e.g., 'listen' and 'silent')[cite: 18]. While sorting both character arrays takes $O(N \log N)$ time, a frequency array achieves $O(N)$ linear time complexity[cite: 18]. After confirming both strings have equal lengths, a single 256-element frequency array is updated in one pass: characters from the first string increment their count (`freq[s1.charAt(i)]++`), while characters from the second string decrement their count (`freq[s2.charAt(i)]--`)[cite: 14, 18]. If the strings are anagrams, every bucket in the frequency array balances to exactly zero[cite: 18].
hints: If `s1.length() != s2.length()`, return `false` immediately[cite: 9, 18].
Use a single `int[] counts = new int[256];` array[cite: 14, 17].
Increment counts for characters in `s1`, decrement for `s2`, and verify that all counts remain zero[cite: 14, 18].
questions.expectedOutput:
Testing 'listen' and 'silent':
Is anagram: true

questions.title: Immutable Class with Defensive Copying
questions.question: Implement an immutable `UserProfile` class with private final fields, no mutators, and defensive copying for mutable fields like `java.util.Date` and arrays[cite: 10, 18].
questions.explanation: Creating a fully immutable class requires more than marking fields `final`[cite: 6, 10]. If a class holds references to mutable objects (such as `Date` or arrays), external callers can modify the internal object state through those references even if the fields themselves cannot be reassigned[cite: 5, 10]. To ensure immutability: 1) Declare the class `final` so subclasses cannot override methods to introduce mutable state[cite: 5]. 2) Make all fields `private final`[cite: 6, 10]. 3) In the constructor, make defensive copies of any mutable arguments before storing them[cite: 10]. 4) In accessor methods, return new copies of mutable fields rather than the internal references[cite: 10].
hints: Defensively copy incoming mutable objects in the constructor: `this.date = new Date(d.getTime());`[cite: 10].
Return new copies from getters: `return new Date(this.date.getTime());`[cite: 10].
Verify that mutating the external Date object does not change the internal state of the immutable instance[cite: 10].
questions.expectedOutput: Internal date preserved: true

questions.title: String HashCode Algorithm and Collision Analysis
questions.question: Implement the standard Java String hash code formula $s[0]\times 31^{n-1} + \dots + s[n-1]$ manually, verify it matches `hashCode()`, and demonstrate hash collisions with 'Aa' and 'BB'.
questions.explanation: Java computes string hash codes using the formula: $h = \sum_{i=0}^{n-1} s[i] \times 31^{n-1-i}$, evaluated using 32-bit signed integer arithmetic where overflow is allowed to wrap around[cite: 5]. Horner's method optimizes this computation iteratively: `h = 31 * h + charAt(i)`[cite: 18]. The multiplier 31 is chosen because it is an odd prime, reducing hash collisions, and can be optimized by compilers into a fast bit-shift and subtraction: `31 * h == (h << 5) - h`[cite: 7]. Because hash codes compress an infinite space of strings into $2^{32}$ integers, collisions can occur[cite: 5]. For example, in 'Aa' and 'BB': $'A' \times 31 + 'a' = 65 \times 31 + 97 = 2112$, and $'B' \times 31 + 'b' = 66 \times 31 + 66 = 2112$, demonstrating a direct collision[cite: 5].
hints: Implement Horner's rule iteratively: `h = 31 * h + s.charAt(i)`[cite: 18].
Verify your manual hash calculation matches `s.hashCode()`[cite: 18].
Confirm that `"Aa".hashCode() == "BB".hashCode()` produces identical hash codes[cite: 18].

Library hashCode('Aa'): 2112
Library hashCode('BB'): 2112

questions.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
questions.question: Find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters in a string using the sliding window technique in $O(N)$ time.
questions.explanation: Finding the longest substring without repeating characters uses a sliding window with two pointers[cite: 14]. An array `lastSeen` sized to 256 stores the most recent index where each character was observed. The pointer `right` expands the window rightward[cite: 14]. If the character `s.charAt(right)` was seen inside the current window (`lastSeen[ch] >= left`), the left boundary advances past the previous occurrence: `left = lastSeen[ch] + 1`[cite: 14]. On each step, `maxLen = Math.max(maxLen, right - left + 1)` updates the maximum length, and `lastSeen[ch] = right` records the current position[cite: 3, 14]. This processes each character at most twice, achieving optimal $O(N)$ linear time complexity[cite: 14].
hints: Use an `int[] lastPos = new int[256];` array initialized to `-1`[cite: 14].
When `lastPos[ch] >= left`, advance `left = lastPos[ch] + 1` to skip the duplicate[cite: 14].
Update the maximum length on every step: `maxLen = Math.max(maxLen, right - left + 1)`[cite: 3, 14].
questions.expectedOutput:
Input: abcabcbb
Longest unique substring length: 3

questions.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
questions.question: Given a string, find the longest contiguous palindromic substring by expanding around potential centers in $O(N^2)$ time and $O(1)$ auxiliary space.
questions.explanation: A palindrome reads identically forward and backward and mirrors around its center[cite: 12, 18]. In a string of length $N$, there are $2N - 1$ potential centers: $N$ odd-length centers (centered on a single character `s[i]`) and $N - 1$ even-length centers (centered between adjacent characters `s[i]` and `s[i+1]`)[cite: 18]. The algorithm iterates through each center, expanding outward with two pointers while characters match (`s[left] == s[right]`)[cite: 9, 14, 18]. If the expanded palindrome exceeds the longest found so far, its boundaries are updated[cite: 3]. This approach runs in $O(N^2)$ time and requires $O(1)$ auxiliary space, avoiding the $O(N^2)$ memory overhead of a 2D dynamic programming table.
hints: Expand around center with a helper method: `expand(s, i, i)` for odd palindromes and `expand(s, i, i + 1)` for even palindromes[cite: 9, 18].
Keep track of the start index and maximum length found so far[cite: 3, 14].
Extract the final longest palindrome using `.substring(start, start + maxLen)`[cite: 3, 18].

Input: babad
Longest Palindromic Substring: bab

questions.title: Custom String Memory Profiler
questions.question: Demonstrate the memory and allocation penalty of string concatenation (`+=`) in a loop versus using a pre-sized `StringBuilder`.
questions.explanation: Because `String` objects are immutable, repeated concatenation inside loops creates substantial garbage collection pressure[cite: 2, 3, 18]. Writing `str += token` inside a loop of $N$ iterations allocates an intermediate `StringBuilder`, appends the string, and allocates a new `String` object via `toString()` on every cycle[cite: 1, 3]. For 10,000 iterations, this allocates thousands of transient byte arrays on the heap, triggering frequent garbage collection cycles[cite: 1, 2]. In contrast, a pre-sized `StringBuilder(capacity)` allocates its backing buffer upfront, appending characters in-place with zero intermediate allocations[cite: 3, 15]. Measuring heap usage highlights the memory efficiency of mutable buffers for sequential text construction[cite: 2, 3].
hints: Inspect heap memory using `Runtime.getRuntime().totalMemory() - Runtime.getRuntime().freeMemory()`[cite: 1, 2].
Run `System.gc()` before each test to establish a clean memory baseline[cite: 2].
Compare the heap memory used by repeated `+=` concatenation versus a pre-sized `StringBuilder`[cite: 2, 3].
questions.expectedOutput:
Pre-sized StringBuilder character count: 5000
Memory profile: Pre-sized StringBuilder executes with minimal heap churn.

questions.title: Minimum Window Substring
questions.question: Given strings $S$ and $T$, find the minimum window substring in $S$ that contains all characters of $T$ in $O(N)$ time using a two-pointer sliding window.
questions.explanation: Finding the minimum window substring uses a two-pointer sliding window with character frequency tracking[cite: 14]. A frequency map `targetMap` stores the character counts of $T$. The pointer `right` expands the window over $S$, updating character counts in `windowMap`[cite: 14]. A counter `matched` tracks how many unique characters in the window satisfy their required frequency in $T$. Once `matched == targetMap.size()`, the window contains all characters of $T$. The pointer `left` then advances rightward to shrink the window while maintaining the match, updating the minimum window length found[cite: 14]. This two-pointer approach examines each character at most twice, achieving optimal $O(|S| + |T|)$ linear time complexity[cite: 14].
hints: Store character requirements of $T$ in a frequency map or array[cite: 14].
Expand the right boundary until all characters from $T$ are present in the window[cite: 14].
Contract the left boundary to minimize window size while preserving the match condition[cite: 14].

Source: ADOBECODEBANC | Target: ABC
Minimum Window Substring: BANC

questions.title: Wildcard String Matching Engine
questions.question: Implement a wildcard pattern matcher supporting `'?'` (matches any single character) and `'*'` (matches any sequence of characters, including empty) in $O(M \times N)$ time.
questions.explanation: Wildcard pattern matching can be implemented cleanly using two-pointer tracking with backtracking. Pointers `sIdx` and `pIdx` track positions in the string and pattern. If characters match directly or the pattern has `'?'`, both pointers advance[cite: 16]. If the pattern has `'*'`, its position is recorded (`starIdx = pIdx`), along with the current string position (`matchIdx = sIdx`), and the pattern pointer advances (`pIdx++`)[cite: 16]. If a mismatch occurs later, the algorithm backtracks: `starIdx` lets `'*'` absorb one more character from the string by updating `matchIdx++`, and `pIdx` resets to `starIdx + 1`. This greedy backtracking approach avoids full dynamic programming table allocation while matching wildcard patterns efficiently[cite: 9, 16].
hints: Advance both pointers when `p.charAt(pIdx) == '?'` or characters match[cite: 16].
When encountering `'*'`, record `starIdx = pIdx` and `matchIdx = sIdx` for backtracking[cite: 16].
On mismatch, backtrack if an active `'*'` exists by advancing the string match index[cite: 16].

Matching 'abcdef' against pattern 'a?c*f':
Result: true
